items.readable_text:
Content:
If we have rational expressions on both sides of an equation, say,
[MATH: \dfrac{{\color{red}x-1}}{{\color{blue}2}} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}2x-1}}{{\color{red}5}},]
then we can eliminate the rational expressions by applying cross-multiplication:

Content:
- we cross-multiply the left-hand side numerator [MATH: ({\color{red}x-1})] with the right-hand side denominator [MATH: ({\color{red}5}),] and
- we cross-multiply the left-hand side denominator [MATH: ({\color{blue}2})] with the right-hand side numerator [MATH: ({\color{blue}2x-1}).]

Content:
Doing this, we get the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: ({\color{red}x-1}) \cdot ({\color{red}5}) = ({\color{blue}2}) \cdot ({\color{blue}2x - 1})]

Content:
After we've cross-multiplied, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:
[MATH: (x − 1) ⋅ 5|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1); 5x − 5|= 4x − 2; 5x − 5 + 5|= 4x − 2 + 5; 5x|= 4x + 3; 5x − 4x|= 4x + 3 − 4x; x|= 3]

Content:
Note: Cross-multiplication might seem magical, but it is really just a shortcut for multiplying both sides of the equation by each denominator:

Content:
[MATH: (x − 1)/(2)|= (2x − 1)/(5); 2 ⋅ (x − 1)/(2)|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5); 2 ⋅ (x − 1)/(2)|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5); x − 1|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5); (x − 1) ⋅ 5|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5) ⋅ 5; (x − 1) ⋅ 5|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5) ⋅ 5; (x − 1) ⋅ (5)|= (2) ⋅ (2x − 1)]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{x+1}{2} = -\dfrac{x}{3}]

Content:
Even though one of the fractions is negative, we can still use cross-multiplication. All we have to do is transfer the negative into the numerator of the fraction, and proceed with cross-multiplication:

Content:
[MATH: (x + 1)/(2)|= − (x)/(3); (x + 1)/(2)|= (− x)/(3); (x + 1) ⋅ 3|= 2 ⋅ (− x)]

Content:
Then, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

Content:
[MATH: (x + 1) ⋅ 3|= 2 ⋅ (− x); 3x + 3|= − 2x; 3x + 3 − 3x|= − 2x − 3x; 3|= − 5x; (3)/(− 5)|= (− 5x)/(− 5); − (3)/(5)|= x]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: x = -\dfrac{3}{5}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If we have rational expressions on both sides of an equation, say,
[MATH: \dfrac{{\color{red}x-1}}{{\color{blue}2}} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}2x-1}}{{\color{red}5}},]
then we can eliminate the rational expressions by applying cross-multiplication:

Content:
- we cross-multiply the left-hand side numerator [MATH: ({\color{red}x-1})] with the right-hand side denominator [MATH: ({\color{red}5}),] and
- we cross-multiply the left-hand side denominator [MATH: ({\color{blue}2})] with the right-hand side numerator [MATH: ({\color{blue}2x-1}).]

Content:
Doing this, we get the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: ({\color{red}x-1}) \cdot ({\color{red}5}) = ({\color{blue}2}) \cdot ({\color{blue}2x - 1})]

Content:
After we've cross-multiplied, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:
[MATH: (x − 1) ⋅ 5|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1); 5x − 5|= 4x − 2; 5x − 5 + 5|= 4x − 2 + 5; 5x|= 4x + 3; 5x − 4x|= 4x + 3 − 4x; x|= 3]

Content:
Note: Cross-multiplication might seem magical, but it is really just a shortcut for multiplying both sides of the equation by each denominator:

Content:
[MATH: (x − 1)/(2)|= (2x − 1)/(5); 2 ⋅ (x − 1)/(2)|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5); 2 ⋅ (x − 1)/(2)|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5); x − 1|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5); (x − 1) ⋅ 5|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5) ⋅ 5; (x − 1) ⋅ 5|= 2 ⋅ (2x − 1)/(5) ⋅ 5; (x − 1) ⋅ (5)|= (2) ⋅ (2x − 1)]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Cross-Multiplying with a Negative Sign

Content:
Consider the following equation:

Even though one of the fractions is negative, we can still use cross-multiplication. All we have to do is transfer the negative into the numerator of the fraction, and proceed with cross-multiplication:
